scope.end: 5b: the garment oath's wording settled ("All of it is mine, but by your ruling…")

sections.title: *Heilakh*: Does "Here You Are" Still Require an Oath?
sections.gist: Continuing the dispute between Rav Sheshet (exempt) and R. Chiya (obligated) over a defendant who hands over what he admits. Three tests fail to settle it: the Mishnah of vessels and land, the verse that excludes land, and Rami bar Chama's baraita on bailees.

children.title: Vessels and Land (*Shevuot* 38b): Proof for *Heilakh*, or Land Bound to the Oath?
children.gist: A Mishnah seems to imply that "here you are" obligates an oath. The Gemara answers that it chose land to teach that land is bound to an oath owed on vessels.

bullets.text: Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman objects to Rav Sheshet from a Mishnah (*Shevuot* 38b). A claim of vessels and land: if he admits the vessels and denies the land, or admits the land and denies the vessels, he is exempt. If he admits part of the land, he is exempt. If he admits part of the vessels, he must swear on the rest.

Inference: he is exempt only because land is not subject to an oath. So a claim of vessels and vessels, set up in the same way, would oblige an oath. That can only be a case where he says "here you are", so *heilakh* obligates, as R. Chiya holds.

Land has two features: it is excluded from oaths, and admitting it is always effectively "here you are", since it can't be moved or hidden. So the Mishnah's choice of land invites the question of which feature is doing the work.

Answer: vessels and vessels would also be exempt. The Mishnah uses land for another lesson: once he admits part of the vessels and must swear, he must also swear on the land he denied, although land alone carries no oath.
This is *gilgul shevuah*: an oath owed on one claim draws in a claim that could not bring an oath on its own.

chart.caption: The Mishnah of vessels and land (*Shevuot* 38b)
rows: Admits the vessels, denies the land
Land is not subject to an oath
Admits the land, denies the vessels
Land is not subject to an oath
Land is not subject to an oath
Must swear on the vessels, and on the land too
Admission and denial are both in vessels; the land is bound to that oath

children.title: Binding (*Zokekin*): Why *Shevuot* Repeats *Kiddushin*
children.gist: The law of binding is already taught in *Kiddushin*. The Gemara explains that *Shevuot* is its main place and *Kiddushin* cites it only in passing.

bullets.text: Challenge: binding is already taught in *Kiddushin* 26a. When a person is obligated to swear about movable property (which does not serve as a guarantee), it binds (*zokekin*) the land (which does) to the same oath. Why repeat it in *Shevuot*?
Answer: *Shevuot*, which deals with oaths, is the main place for this law. *Kiddushin* cites it incidentally, in its survey of how the two kinds of property differ.
*Kiddushin*'s concern there is modes of acquisition, so the oath law comes up only as an aside.

children.title: Why a Verse to Exempt Land? Dug-Up Land, or Land Denied
children.gist: If *heilakh* is exempt, and admitting land is always "here you are", the verse excluding land seems unneeded. Two answers show cases where land is not "here you are".

bullets.text: Question on Rav Sheshet: why must Shemot 22:8 exclude land from the oath of *modeh be'miktzat*? Land stays where it is, so every admission of land is "here you are", which he already exempts.
Answer 1: the defendant dug pits, ditches and caves in the land. It is damaged and not in its former state, so returning it is not "here you are".
Answer 2: a claim of vessels and land, where he admits the vessels and denies the land. Nothing is handed over regarding the land, yet the verse teaches that he does not swear on it.
Land counts as "here you are" only when it is admitted. When land is the denied part, only the verse can exempt it.

children.title: Rami bar Chama's Four Bailees: Items Returned, or Three Dead Cows?
children.gist: A baraita requiring bailees to admit part and deny part seems to describe "here you are". The Gemara recasts it as a bailee who admits paying for a dead cow.

bullets.text: Proof for R. Chiya: Rami bar Chama's baraita says all four bailees (unpaid, borrower, paid, renter) must deny part of the claim and admit part in order to be liable to swear.
What is the case? Presumably: "What I admit receiving, here you are. The rest I never received." So *heilakh* obligates an oath.
A deposit is an object that still exists, so admitting it naturally means handing it over. A loan is different: the money is spent and not presumed to be at hand.

Rejected: the depositor says, "I gave you three cows, and all died through your negligence." The unpaid bailee answers: "One never happened. One died by accident. One died through my negligence, and I will pay for it." That is *modeh be'miktzat*, but not "here you are": no cow is returned.
The admission is a debt of money for the dead cow. The claim that one died by accident is the bailee's own exemption, folded into the same oath.

sections.title: Witnesses to Part of the Claim: R. Chiya's First *Halakha* Tested
sections.gist: First a baraita that seems to exclude witnesses, answered by how each tanna reads "this is it". Then the rule is applied to a shepherd caught eating two animals: who swears when he can't, whether Rav Nachman's oath would do the same, and why being a shepherd did not already disqualify him.

children.title: The Baraita of R. Aptoriki's Father: "By His Mouth, Not by Witnesses"
children.gist: A baraita excludes witnesses from the oath of partial admission. R. Chiya, himself a tanna, reads the verse's double wording as requiring an admission of the same kind instead.

children.title: Witnesses Excluded by the Verse, but R. Chiya Is a Tanna
children.gist: The baraita derives from the verse that witnesses to part do not oblige an oath. R. Chiya may dispute it, reading the verse as teaching only the basic oath.

bullets.text: The father of R. Aptoriki teaches: A claims 100 dinars, B says "nothing of yours is with me", and witnesses testify that B owes 50. One might think B swears on the rest.
The verse says "about which one shall say: This is it" (Shemot 22:8). The oath comes from an admission by his own mouth, not from the testimony of witnesses.
Answer: R. Chiya is himself a tanna, and may dispute a baraita.
But the baraita cites a verse! For R. Chiya, the verse teaches only that one who admits part must swear.
R. Chiya's own rule rests on a *kal va'chomer*: if his own admission of part obliges an oath on the rest, witnesses, who have no stake and carry more weight, should do so all the more.
R. Chiya belonged to the last generation of tanna'im, which is why he can stand against a baraita.

children.title: "This" and "It": Excluding Witnesses, or Requiring the Same Kind?
children.gist: Both tanna'im read two lessons from "this is it". They differ on the second: the father of R. Aptoriki excludes witnesses, R. Chiya requires an admission of the kind claimed, as in the wheat-and-barley Mishnah.

bullets.text: The father of R. Aptoriki: "this is it" (*ki hu zeh*) has two words. One teaches the oath of *modeh be'miktzat*, and the other exempts where witnesses testify.
R. Chiya: one word teaches the basic oath, and the other requires that the admission be of the same kind as the claim (*min ha'ta'anah*). If he admits a different kind, he does not swear.

The father of R. Aptoriki does not require the same kind; he holds like Rabban Gamliel. Mishnah (*Shevuot* 38b): claimed wheat, admitted barley, which is cheaper. The first tanna exempts him; Rabban Gamliel obliges an oath.
For Rabban Gamliel, what counts is value: a claim worth more, partly admitted with something worth less, is partial admission and partial denial even though the items differ.

chart.caption: How each tanna reads the two words of "this is it"
rows: Admission must be of the same kind

children.title: R. Zeira and Abaye: A Proven Robber, So the Owners Swear and Collect
children.gist: By R. Chiya's rule the shepherd owes an oath on the rest; since a proven robber can't swear, the owners swear and collect.

bullets.text: A shepherd was given animals every day in front of witnesses. One day they gave them without witnesses. At the end of the day he said: "This never happened." Witnesses testified that he ate two of them.
Tosafot: the daily witnesses were also there to prove that the deposit had been received, so that he could not later claim he had already returned it.
R. Zeira: if R. Chiya's first *halakha* holds, the shepherd must swear on the rest or pay.
Abaye: swear? He is a robber! The witnesses proved he took and ate the animals, so his oath has no credibility.
R. Zeira: I meant that the opposing party swears and collects (*nishba ve'notel*).

Tosafot: sometimes the other side swears and collects, and sometimes one who can't swear simply pays (*mitokh she'eino yakhol lishava meshalem*). If a man permanently disqualified from oaths simply paid, anyone could press a claim on him, so the claimant must swear. And he is willing to swear; it is the court that refuses his oath. By contrast, one who can't swear because he doesn't know the facts pays.

children.title: Rav Nachman's *Shevuat Heset*: No Ordinance upon an Ordinance
children.gist: Even without R. Chiya, Rav Nachman's oath for one who denies everything might have the owners swear. Both steps are rabbinic, and one ordinance is not built on another.

bullets.text: Challenge: even if the *halakha* is not like R. Chiya, the shepherd denied everything and so owes Rav Nachman's oath. He can't swear, so the owners should swear and collect.
Source: Mishnah (*Shevuot* 38b), a claim of 100 answered by "nothing of yours is with me" is exempt. Rav Nachman: the judges still impose a *shevuat heset*.

Answer: Rav Nachman's oath is a rabbinic ordinance, not a Torah oath. The rule that the plaintiff swears and collects when the defendant is suspect regarding oaths is also rabbinic. *Takanta le'takanta lo avdinan*: we do not institute one ordinance upon another, so no oath is imposed.

A Torah oath is the defendant's own way of freeing himself, so if he can't take it, shifting it to the other side follows naturally. Rav Nachman's oath is a deterrent against false denial, and his failure to take it should not empower the claimant.

children.title: Why Not Disqualify Him as a Shepherd? His Own Flock vs. Others'
children.gist: Rav Yehuda disqualifies an ordinary shepherd, but only one herding his own animals. One who herds others' animals is not presumed to steal.

bullets.text: Question: why rest the shepherd's disqualification on the robbery? R. Zeira could have said he is disqualified as a shepherd: Rav Yehuda says an ordinary shepherd is disqualified, presumed a robber because he grazes his animals in other people's fields.
Answer: Rav Yehuda means one who herds his own animals. This shepherd herded animals belonging to others.
Otherwise, how could anyone give his animals to a shepherd? It would violate "Do not put a stumbling block before the blind" (Vayikra 19:14, *lifnei iver*).
The presumption is that a person sins only for his own benefit, and he will not rob for animals that are not his.
So this shepherd's disqualification needed the witnesses who saw him eat two; his trade alone did not establish it.

sections.title: The Garment Oath: "All Mine", "Half Mine", or Rav Huna's Formula
sections.gist: Returning to the chapter's opening Mishnah on two holding a garment, the Gemara fixes each one's oath. Rav Huna adds "I have a claim to it", and the Gemara shows why neither "all of it" nor "half of it" will do.

bullets.text: Mishnah: each swears that he has no less than half of it, and they divide it.
Question: does he swear about what he has, or about what he does not have? "I don't have less than half" could be said by one with no claim at all.
One who owns nothing could say, without lying, that what he has is "not less than half", since there is nothing there to fall short.
Rav Huna: he swears, "I have a claim to it, and I do not have a claim to less than half of it."
Why not swear "all of it is mine", which is his claim? Would we give him all of it? The court should not administer an oath to a claim it will not award.
If the court had him swear to the whole and then gave him half, it would appear to act against the oath it had just accepted.
Why not swear "half of it is mine"? That would compromise his own claim that it is all his.
Challenge: Rav Huna's formula also seems to concede half. Answer: he says, "All of it is mine; but by your ruling, I swear that I have a claim to it, and not less than half."
"No less than half" sets a floor, not a ceiling, so it is fully consistent with owning the whole garment.

sections.continues: Continues at 5b.8: why an oath is needed at all when each keeps what he holds (R. Yochanan: an ordinance so that people won't seize others' garments), and whether one suspect regarding money is suspect regarding oaths.

key_terms.sense: handing over the admitted part of a claim
key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of a claim and says of the admitted portion "here it is", presenting or handing it over. Whether such an admission still obliges an oath on the denied remainder is disputed.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Sheshet exempts and R. Chiya obligates. The Mishnah of vessels and land, the verse excluding land, and Rami bar Chama's baraita are each read so as not to decide the question.

key_terms.sense: partial admission obliging a Torah oath
key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of a monetary claim and denies the rest must take a Torah oath on the part he denies.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks what counts as partial admission: handing over the admitted item, a bailee's admission of negligence, witnesses to part, or an admission of a different kind.

key_terms.sense: binding a further claim to an oath already owed
key_terms.definition: Once a defendant must swear on one claim, other claims can be attached to that oath, including claims such as land that would carry no oath on their own. Also called gilgul shevuah.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah in *Shevuot* uses land to teach that an oath owed on vessels binds the land too; the Gemara explains why that Mishnah repeats *Kiddushin*.

key_terms.sense: an admission of the kind claimed
key_terms.definition: The requirement that a partial admission concern the same kind of thing as the claim, so that admitting a different item (barley for wheat) is not partial admission.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Chiya derives it from one word of "this is it"; the father of R. Aptoriki, holding like Rabban Gamliel, does not require it.

key_terms.definition: Cases in which the plaintiff, rather than the defendant, takes the oath and thereby collects; among them, where the defendant owes an oath but is disqualified from swearing.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Zeira applies it to the shepherd proven a robber; the Gemara calls the rule rabbinic, so it is not stacked on Rav Nachman's rabbinic oath.

key_terms.sense: rabbinic oath for one who denies everything
key_terms.definition: An oath instituted by Rav Nachman for a defendant who denies a claim entirely, who is exempt from any Torah oath.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Because it is rabbinic, a shepherd unable to take it does not trigger the claimant's swearing and collecting, which is also rabbinic.

judgment_calls: The question of why a verse is needed to exempt land (5a.1–3) could stand as its own section; kept under the *heilakh* debate because it is a challenge to Rav Sheshet's view that *heilakh* is exempt.

The *Kiddushin* question (4b.14–15) could be a child of the vessels-and-land section, since it challenges that section's answer; made a sibling because it is a separate question about the Mishnah's redundancy.
Rami bar Chama's baraita (5a.4–6) is placed under the *heilakh* debate, not under R. Chiya's first *halakha*, because it is brought as a proof for his *heilakh* view.

The shepherd case could be its own top-level section; nested under R. Chiya's first *halakha* because R. Zeira frames it explicitly by that *halakha*, with Rav Nachman's oath and the shepherd's status as children.
The garment oath is left as one section with no children: its four steps form a single argument, which the chart sets out.
coverage_notes: The essay opens by saying Mar Zutra challenges R. Chiya; the text says he objects to Rav Sheshet, since the inference would support R. Chiya's view that *heilakh* obligates. Followed the text.
The essay says the land exclusion is derived through *klal u'ferat u'klal*; the text here only cites Shemot 22:8. Did not mention the derivation method.

The essay's initial reading of Rami bar Chama's baraita is a three-cow case in which one is admitted and one denied; in the text the initial reading is "what I admit, here you are; the rest I never received", and the three cows appear only in the rejection. Followed the text.

The essay's account of the wheat-and-barley dispute has R. Chiya following Rabban Gamliel; the text says the father of R. Aptoriki holds like Rabban Gamliel, while R. Chiya requires an admission of the same kind. Followed the text.
The *kal va'chomer* for R. Chiya's witness rule is not stated in this daf's text; kept as the lecturer's framing (source: shiur).
The essay says the owners claimed ten sheep and swore to ten; the text gives no number. Omitted the number.

The essay says the rule of the opposing party swearing applies only where the original oath is from the Torah; the text says that rule is itself a rabbinic ordinance, so it is not layered on Rav Nachman's ordinance. Followed the text; the lecturer's Torah/rabbinic contrast is kept as shiur analysis.
4b.11–4b.15 falls on the previous amud but is covered in this daf's shiur, so no section is flagged as text only.
The shiur ends with the garment oath's wording at 5b.7; 5b.8 onward (why an oath at all, and suspicion regarding money versus oaths) falls to the next outline.
